chunks: Al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddiq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār ibn Mūsā al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said:
I asked him about tayammum in place of wudu (ablution), janābah, and menstruation for women—are they the same? He said: “Yes.”

Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: The one who enters a state of ritual impurity through sleep, fainting, and al-mirrah performs tayammum as we mentioned in the chapter of one rendered muḥdith by urine and feces, and by that enters into salat (prayer). If these things are among what nullifies taharah (ritual purity), and the one whose taharah is nullified is required to perform tayammum according to what we have mentioned, then there is no difference between his taharah being nullified by one of these things or by urine and feces, according to what we have mentioned concerning the obligation of tayammum upon him.

Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: Whenever one of those whom we have mentioned finds water after having lacked it, or becomes able to use it, he purifies himself with it according to what he had missed: if it was wudu (ablution), then wudu; and if it was ghusl (ritual bath), then ghusl. The difference between tayammum as a substitute for ghusl and tayammum as a substitute for wudu is what we have explained: that the muḥdith whose purification is required by ghusl, if he is unable to perform it, does tayammum with two strikes, one of them for his face and the second for the back of his hands; while the muḥdith whose purification is required by wudu does tayammum with one strike for his face and his hands. Its explanation has already passed in full, and in it there is sufficiency, if Allah the Exalted wills.

Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: If water is not found for washing the deceased, the Muslim gives him tayammum just as the living person who is incapacitated by chronic illness is given tayammum when he needs tayammum from his janābah: he strikes with his two hands on the earth and wipes with them his face from the hairline of his head to the tip of his nose, then strikes with them another strike and wipes with them the back of his hands. Then he himself performs tayammum for touching him in the same manner equally. What indicates that is what has been established regarding the obligation of ghusl for the deceased and that whoever lacks water, his obligation transfers to tayammum according to what we have stated earlier.

key_terms.التَّيَمُّمِ: dry ablution used as a substitute for ritual purification when water is unavailable or unusable
key_terms.الْجَنَابَةِ: state of major ritual impurity requiring ghusl
key_terms.الْحَيْضِ: menstruation, after which ritual purification is required
key_terms.الْوُضُوءِ: minor ritual purification required for certain acts of worship

ai.seo_question: What are the rulings for tayammum in place of wudu (ablution), ghusl, and for the deceased when water is unavailable?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses the legal rulings of tayammum as a substitute for wudu (ablution) and ghusl (ritual bath), including for janābah, menstruation, and other states that nullify taharah (ritual purity). It explains when tayammum is performed, the difference between tayammum replacing ghusl and tayammum replacing wudu, and the ruling for the deceased when water is unavailable.
